title: When Timbot Glitched, These MIT Students Turned a Tech Fail into a Teaching Moment
summary:
Picture this: you’re at a national robotics tournament, surrounded by high school teams from all 50 states, and your robot—the one you built in a frantic three-day sprint—suddenly won’t move. That’s exactly what happened to MIT’s FIRSTxMIT club at the Governors Cup in Washington, D.C. Their robot, Timbot, was hit with Wi-Fi issues. Instead of panicking, the team sat cross-legged on the floor and started troubleshooting. As they worked, curious high schoolers gathered. “We ended up tethering the robot with a long Ethernet cable, instead of using wireless, and a lot of students were like, ‘whoa, we do that too!’” said first-year Lily Sand. The glitch became an instant bonding moment.

FIRSTxMIT is a new campus club for alumni of FIRST Robotics, a program that has deep roots at MIT. Inventor Dean Kamen and the late Professor Woodie Flowers launched the FIRST Robotics Competition in 1992, inspired by Flowers’ iconic mechanical engineering class. Today, an estimated 15–20% of MIT undergrads participated in FIRST. Co-founders Debbie Ang and Perry Han, both sophomores, started the club to channel that shared passion into outreach. Their kickoff event drew 185 students.

Building Timbot in 72 hours for the Robot in 3 Days challenge was a feat—high school teams typically take six weeks. At the Governors Cup, the club demonstrated the robot, staffed an MIT Admissions booth, and mingled with governors, including Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey. “Having MIT students tell the story of the power of FIRST is incredibly compelling,” said advisor Trinidad Carney. Han recalls speaking with an Ohio state senator: “It really showed me that, when you have people in government that are excited about STEM education, it can really go places.” The club now plans to expand, aiming to put robots in more students’ hands and show that STEM is about building, not just textbooks.
why_it_matters: The experience demonstrates that even elite students encounter setbacks, and that sharing those moments can demystify STEM and encourage younger peers to embrace engineering. It also underscores how student-driven outreach can influence education policy by connecting with government officials.

background_read: FIRST (For Inspiration and Recognition of Science and Technology) was founded in 1989 by inventor Dean Kamen—best known for the Segway—and MIT professor emeritus Woodie Flowers, a beloved figure in engineering education. The FIRST Robotics Competition launched in 1992, challenging high school teams to build robots in six weeks using a standard kit of parts.

MIT has long been a hub for FIRST; many MIT students are alumni, and the institute hosts regional events. The Robot in 3 Days challenge, where Timbot was built, is a condensed version that tests rapid prototyping and teamwork, mirroring real-world engineering pressures.

At the Governors Cup, held in Washington, D.C., the club also met Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey, a Democrat who has championed STEM education and workforce development. The event illustrates how robotics competitions can connect students with policymakers, potentially influencing funding for STEM programs. FIRST has grown into a global movement, with events in over 100 countries, and its alumni network includes countless professionals in science and technology fields.

perspectives.description: The quick thinking to tether the robot and the spontaneous gathering of students turned a potential embarrassment into a powerful teaching moment. It proves that failures are a critical part of learning and that transparency can build community and trust in STEM fields.

Reliance on a frantic 72-hour build could lead to instability; perhaps a more structured, longer preparation might have prevented the glitch. Also, the need for an Ethernet cable in a wireless era highlights technological vulnerabilities that teams must address.

The event reflects a broader pattern in STEM education: high-pressure competitions that mimic real engineering crises help students develop resilience and problem-solving skills. The involvement of politicians also illustrates how grassroots STEM enthusiasm can translate into policy support for educational funding.

As FIRSTxMIT plans to expand, it could create a model for university-led STEM mentorship that reaches underserved schools, potentially diversifying the engineering pipeline. Future events might integrate more wireless reliability testing, leading to even more robust robot designs.
